newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rhone-Poulenc plans Rorer buyout, unit spinoff.
newsitem.headline: Rhone-Poulenc plans Rorer buyout, unit spinoff.

text.p: Drugs and chemicals giant Rhone-Poulenc said Thursday it planned to launch a 25 billion franc ($4.3 billion) buyout bid for U.S.-based pharmaceutical company Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, in which it holds a 68 percent stake.

Rhone-Poulenc said it would pay Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's shareholders $92 a share in the deal. RPR stock, which closed at $79.44 Wednesday, shot up to $90.625 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange after an initial brief trading halt.
The French company also said it would regroup its chemical and fiber operations into a single unit that will be partly spun off and taken public in 1998.
It said it would retain majority control of the new unit but did not specify how much it would keep.
The moves were meant to boost Rhone-Poulenc's competitive muscle in the global chemicals and pharmaceuticals industry, which has been swept by a wave of big mergers.
"The logic is clear," Chairman Jean-Rene Fourtou said. "It is to become a strong worldwide company in life sciences."
He said the buyout of RPR, which is based in Collegeville, Pa., would give Rhone-Poulenc the means for future expansion.

"Our developement is internally based, but we do not exclude in time participating in other strategic movements. This deal allows us to envision movements that until now would have been impossible," Fourtou told a news conference.
"Alliances are just starting to happen in the chemicals sector. Greater autonomy should allow (the new company) to participate ... if the opportunity presents itself.
Analysts were enthusiastic about the plans, which they said made strategic sense and would boost Rhone-Poulenc's price-to-earnings ratio.
They were also in line with Rhone-Poulenc's aims to focus on its lucrative pharmaceuticals business.

Fourtou said the company stopped short of an outright bid for RPR because under a 1990 standstill agreement Rhone-Poulenc cannot increase its holding in RPR until after July 31, 1997, and because Rhone had not yet completed its study of the deal's merits.
But he said the only risks to completing the deal were a rise in the RPR share price to over $92 or collapse of the French stock market, both of which he said were unlikely.
He added that the regrouping of the chemicals and fiber divisions would occur regardless of the outcome of its offer for RPR.
